title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2311
summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia with 23 aboard, crashed north of Brunswick, Georgia on April 5, 1991 during approach to landing. The NTSB investigation determined that the left propeller control unit malfunctioned, allowing the left propeller to overspeed with its blades oriented nearly perpendicular to the direction of flight. This created severe asymmetric thrust with insufficient thrust on the left side, causing a left roll that exceeded pilot recovery capability. The crew did not perceive the problem until the propeller blade angle reached 22-26 degrees, at which point the aircraft became very difficult to control.
probable_cause: A malfunction of the left propeller control unit allowed the left propeller to overspeed, creating severe asymmetric thrust that rolled the aircraft to the left beyond the pilot's control authority to recover.

factors.evidence: Propeller control unit malfunction allowed left propeller to overspeed with blades nearly perpendicular to direction of flight, creating asymmetric thrust condition.
Crew was unable to perceive problem until propeller blade angle reached 22-26 degrees; aircraft became very difficult to control at that point.
Aircraft was in approach phase during descent to landing when propeller malfunction developed at critical phase with high workload.
Aircraft rolled to the left until wings were perpendicular to ground; descended in nose-down attitude and disappeared behind trees near airport.
Aircraft struck ground in nose-down attitude after rolling left and losing control during approach.

events.text: Flight 2311 departed Atlanta at 13:47, 23 minutes behind schedule, with no reported mechanical problems after performing round trip to Montgomery.
Just after 14:48, flight crew acknowledged to Jacksonville ATC that airport was in sight and was cleared for visual approach to runway 7.
Last transmission reported to ASA manager; propeller control unit failure caused left propeller overspeed with blades nearly perpendicular at low altitude during approach.
Aircraft suddenly rolled to the left until wings were perpendicular to ground; descended in nose-down attitude and disappeared behind trees near airport.
